overview: Oyo was a powerful Yoruba kingdom and empire whose cavalry, markets and tributary relationships connected northern Yorubaland with routes toward the Atlantic. Its history includes both the older capital, Oyo-Ile, and a smaller kingdom rebuilt farther south after the imperial collapse. The map’s broad coverage should not be read as one unchanged empire lasting to 1914.

periods.title: Imperial Oyo
periods.summary: Oyo expanded through warfare, tribute and commerce; its reach varied, and the slave trade formed part of its economy.

periods.title: Civil war and the loss of the old capital
periods.summary: Internal conflict and the rise of Ilorin shattered the empire; the capital was abandoned around 1836.

periods.title: A rebuilt kingdom and continuing Yoruba communities
periods.summary: A new Oyo arose well south of Oyo-Ile, while the former empire’s communities followed different political paths.

sections.title: An actual city, built room by room

items.text: Brian Hallam’s survey of Oyo-Ile records a palace made of many courtyards surrounded by rooms. Compounds belonging to leading chiefs stood nearby. A palace was a whole neighborhood of activities, rather than one throne room.

South of that palace was a large water reservoir; to its east lay the Akesan market. The survey describes traders’ booths shaded by trees. Water storage, shopping and royal administration occupied neighboring parts of the city.

At nearby Kosso, surviving walls reached about six metres. Builders laid thick courses of earth and let each dry before adding the next. Archaeologists suggest some high holes held scaffolding, but the holes’ precise uses still need research.

Cooking and serving bowls excavated at Ede-Ile carry potters’ marks. Ogundiran and Saunders studied them across occupations from the early 1600s to the 1820s to investigate how makers and vessels connected households within the empire. An ordinary bowl can preserve a maker’s social world.

Charcoal from Bara’s Oyo-period contexts, dated roughly 1570 to 1835, includes several woodland tree groups, including Terminalia and Senegalia. Families had to obtain suitable fuel before a meal could even begin. These fragments record that work, although they cannot tell us the complete dinner menu.

The Bara study found different proportions of wood in different deposits. Access, season and the tasks being performed may explain the variation. The researchers treat these as possibilities, not proof that every household followed one firewood rule.

Ede-Ile began as an Oyo frontier camp and developed into a town connecting inland routes with the coast. Its clay tobacco pipes document an Atlantic-introduced habit becoming part of local social life during the 1600s to 1800s.

Those pipes resemble examples from Oyo-Ile, but resemblance does not settle where they were made. Ajibade’s chemical study is a step toward identifying production and exchange. Similar-looking pipes need not have come from the same workshop.

sections.title: Family memory and a little written Yoruba

items.text: A later Oyo-Yoruba memorial figure at the Met, dated broadly to the nineteenth or twentieth century, combines carved wood with camwood powder, beads and blueing. Its surface bears evidence of handling, so use and care matter alongside carving skill.

In the tradition described by the museum, a mother bathed, dressed, adorned and ritually fed a figure made after a twin’s death. It remained a relationship with a loved person. These are memorial objects, not evidence that every Yoruba family held identical beliefs.

“Bu omi fun mi ki nmo” means “Give me some water to drink” in Samuel Crowther’s 1852 Yoruba vocabulary. This is Yoruba in the book’s Roman-letter spelling, a later printed witness to the language, not writing copied from an imperial palace wall.

A small sentence can reveal an ordinary concern across centuries: somebody is thirsty. Crowther’s dictionary also supplies practical examples about corn for a horse and yam for a child under the same verb. Language learning did not have to begin with royal proclamations.

Oyo’s collapse was a sequence. Afonja’s rebellion, the Muslim movement at Ilorin and earlier civil wars all mattered. Robin Law dates the old capital’s abandonment to about 1836; rebuilding at modern Oyo preserved kingship without restoring the former empire.

ending.text: The old empire broke apart in the early 1800s and Oyo-Ile was abandoned around 1836. A smaller kingdom was rebuilt farther south. Yoruba people, language and institutions continued; the collapse of imperial power was not their disappearance.
